subsection: 9. Marriage, the family and the changing role of women; affluence, leisure time and the consumer society

notes.h: Background: war, recovery and the starting position of women
notes.b: To understand the changes after 1945, you need to know where families and women started from. Europe was damaged and short of homes, but its economy was about to grow fast, and that growth paid for most of what follows.
points: The Second World War left Europe devastated, with serious housing shortages and millions of men returning from military service, so families had to be rebuilt and homes found for them.

Western Europe's post-war economic growth is what paid for rising incomes, welfare states (governments providing benefits such as family allowances) and the consumer goods that filled homes in the 1950s and 1960s.
Before 1945 most European women had few legal rights in marriage and were paid less than men, which is why later reforms of family law and pay mattered so much.

Women had gained the vote only recently in many countries: French women voted for the first time in 1945, the right having been granted by ordinance in 1944, and Italian women voted in 1946, the right having been granted in 1945.
notes.tip: Use this starting position as the 'before' in any essay on how the role of women changed: legal inequality, lower pay and a very recent vote.

notes.h: Key personality: Simone de Beauvoir (The Second Sex and feminism)
notes.b: De Beauvoir was a French philosopher and writer whose 1949 study The Second Sex became a founding text of modern feminism. Feminism is the argument for equal rights and opportunities for women, and a challenge to the roles society assigns them.
points: She was born in Paris on 9 January 1908 and died there on 14 April 1986. She was a philosopher and writer and the partner of Jean-Paul Sartre, with whom she shared a close intellectual life for decades.

She passed the highly competitive agrégation (the French state examination for teaching posts) in philosophy in 1929, placed second to Sartre and, at 21, the youngest candidate to have passed. She then taught for some years.

The Second Sex (Le Deuxième Sexe) was published in two volumes in 1949 and translated into English in 1953. It argued that women were treated as the 'Other' while men were taken as the norm by a male-centred society.
She argued that women's inferior position was created by history, law, religion and education, not by biology, so it could be changed, and that economic independence was the key for women.
Her best-known line, from The Second Sex, is "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." It separated biological sex from the roles society gives women, which is the idea behind the word gender.

She lived through the Second World War and the Occupation of Paris as a witness. Later she became a participant in the feminist movement of the 1970s, joining the Women's Liberation Movement (MLF) in France and campaigning for the legalisation of abortion.

In April 1971 she signed the Manifesto of the 343, in which women declared that they had had abortions, and she co-founded the pro-choice group Choisir with the lawyer Gisèle Halimi. She did not sponsor the 1975 abortion law.

Contemporaries were divided. The Vatican placed her works, including The Second Sex, on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1956, and male intellectuals on both left and right attacked or mocked it, yet younger women read it as a guide to their own position.

Historians now treat the book as a foundational text of second-wave feminism. Later critics questioned its assumption of a universal experience of womanhood, pointing to differences of class and race.
notes.tip: Examiners ask what The Second Sex argued, its date (1949), her 1970s activism and how people judged it. Give one sentence of argument ('made, not born'), one of impact, and name a reaction such as the Church's condemnation or praise from younger feminists. Do not confuse her with Simone Veil.

notes.h: Post-war family life and the baby boom
notes.b: After 1945 marriage and childbirth rose, and a domestic model of family life became the norm in much of Western Europe. Governments, churches and the media all backed it.
points: The baby boom (a sharp rise in the number of births) in Western Europe ran from about 1946 to the mid-1960s, with birth rates higher than in the 1930s. Marriage was also earlier and more common than before the war.
The nuclear family, meaning two parents and their children, with a male breadwinner and a housewife-mother, became the ideal.
Housing shortages after the war meant that many young couples lived with relatives, so public housing programmes were used to increase family accommodation.
Welfare states paid family allowances (regular payments to families with children), which helped parents afford larger families.
The emphasis on the housewife and mother reflected a wish to restore stability after the war, so conservative parties and churches promoted the family as the basis of society.
Cinema, magazines, television and advertising presented the ideal of the happy housewife surrounded by labour-saving appliances, which reinforced the idea that her place was in the home.

Inside marriage, women were legally unequal. In France a law of 13 July 1965 allowed a married woman to work and open a bank account without her husband's permission, which shows that she needed it until then.
In West Germany the marriage law kept a clause until 1977 that a wife was to run the household and could work only if that was compatible with her family duties.
notes.tip: To show legal inequality, give a dated example such as France, 1965, rather than saying only that married women had fewer rights.

notes.h: Women in the workforce and equal pay
notes.b: From the 1950s more married women took paid jobs, but they were concentrated in low-paid work. Equal pay laws were the first real attempt to close the gap.
points: The number of married women in paid employment rose steadily from the 1950s, especially in service work and clerical (office) work, because these sectors grew as economies expanded.
Women's work was mostly in low-paid jobs such as teaching, nursing, secretarial work and factory assembly, and women were paid less than men and barred from many professions.
Article 119 of the Treaty of Rome (1957) required equal pay for equal work for men and women, but at first it was weakly enforced.

In the second Defrenne case (Defrenne v Sabena), decided on 8 April 1976, the European Court of Justice ruled that Article 119 had direct effect, which means individual women could rely on it in their national courts.
In Britain the Equal Pay Act 1970 came into force on 29 December 1975, alongside the Sex Discrimination Act 1975.
notes.tip: Keep Article 119 (the 1957 treaty text) and the Defrenne case (1976 enforcement) apart. Explain why women's position changed by naming the growth in service jobs and the EEC's equal-pay rule, not only by listing laws.

notes.b: Second-wave feminism of the 1960s and 1970s demanded equal pay, nurseries and an end to confinement in the home. A central demand was control over childbearing, and the pill and new laws made this possible. This is different from first-wave feminism, which won the vote before 1945.
points: The contraceptive pill was approved in the USA in 1960 and became widely used in Western Europe in the 1960s, so women could now plan whether and when to have children.
France legalised contraception with the Neuwirth Law of December 1967, named after Lucien Neuwirth. Do not confuse it with the Veil Law on abortion.
The Veil Law of 17 January 1975 legalised abortion in France within the first ten weeks of pregnancy. It was sponsored by the health minister Simone Veil.

Elsewhere, Britain's Abortion Act of 1967 legalised abortion on medical grounds in England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland. Italy legalised abortion in 1978, and West Germany reformed its abortion law in the 1970s.
The Catholic Church opposed contraception and abortion. Pope Paul VI's encyclical (a formal papal letter) Humanae Vitae in 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception.

Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), an American book, helped start second-wave feminism by arguing that confinement to the home left women unfulfilled. The Mouvement de libération des femmes (MLF) was formed in France in 1970.

The Manifesto of the 343, published in Le Nouvel Observateur in April 1971, carried the names of 343 women who declared that they had had abortions, so it called publicly for legalisation. Choisir, a pro-choice group founded in 1971, continued the campaign.
notes.tip: Examiners reward 'France, 1975' over 'some countries legalised abortion'. Keep Neuwirth (contraception, 1967) separate from Veil (abortion, 1975), and the 1971 Manifesto (women who had abortions) separate from the Veil Law. Britain's Abortion Act (1967) is also not the Divorce Reform Act (1969).

notes.b: From 1969 divorce became easier in several Western European countries, and family law moved from the husband as head of the household towards equality between spouses. Change came at very different speeds.
points: The Divorce Reform Act of 1969 in England and Wales took effect in 1971 and made irretrievable breakdown of the marriage the sole ground for divorce.
Italy legalised divorce in December 1970 under the Fortuna-Baslini law. In a referendum on 12 May 1974 voters chose to keep it, with about 59 per cent against repeal.
Italy's family-law reform of 1975 gave spouses equal rights, replacing the idea of the husband as head of household.

West Germany's marriage and family law reform of 1 July 1977 introduced divorce by breakdown instead of fault, so one partner no longer had to be proved guilty. It also dropped the clause that a wife was to run the household.

Later and slower cases show the influence of the Catholic Church. Spain legalised divorce in 1981, and Ireland, whose constitution banned it, approved divorce only by a narrow referendum vote in November 1995.
Divorce rates rose across the region in the 1970s, and single-parent households became a growing category.
The rise in divorce and in working mothers led to debate about the future of the family, with conservatives blaming the changes on permissiveness.
notes.tip: Keep Italy's divorce law (1970) and the referendum (1974) as two separate dates. State each law with its country and year.

notes.b: Economic growth raised incomes in the 1950s and 1960s. Families could now buy goods once thought luxuries, and this created a consumer society, one built around buying and owning goods, which critics soon attacked.
points: Households acquired consumer durables (goods that last for years), such as refrigerators, washing machines and televisions. These saved housework and changed daily routines.

Cars became affordable: the Volkswagen Beetle, mass-produced in West Germany from the late 1940s, was a huge success in the 1950s and 1960s, the Citroën 2CV was launched in 1948, the Fiat 500 in 1957 and the Mini in 1959.
Self-service supermarkets spread across Western Europe in the 1960s, and they changed how families shopped and the goods available to them.
Hire purchase (paying for goods in instalments) and consumer credit made it possible for families to buy goods before they could afford them outright.
Advertising and television encouraged consumption. Television spread rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, becoming the centre of the home and the main form of evening leisure.
Vance Packard in The Hidden Persuaders (1957) argued that advertising manipulated consumers.
John Kenneth Galbraith in The Affluent Society (1958) argued that private affluence went with public squalor, meaning rich households but poor public services.

Herbert Marcuse in One-Dimensional Man (1964) argued that consumer society encouraged conformity and suppressed critical thought. The French Situationists, whose leader Guy Debord wrote The Society of the Spectacle (1967), also attacked the 'spectacle' of consumption.
notes.tip: Strong answers say what changed (goods, cars, supermarkets, credit), why (growth, wages, credit, advertising, television) and who criticised it. Show that each critic had a different angle: Packard on manipulation, Galbraith on private wealth against public poverty, Marcuse on conformity, Debord on the spectacle.

notes.b: Higher incomes came with more free time. Together they created mass leisure industries, above all mass tourism to the Mediterranean.
points: Working hours fell and paid holidays grew. In France paid holiday was two weeks from 1936, a third week was added in 1956 and a fourth in 1969, so workers had more time away from work.

Package holidays (flights, hotel and transfers sold as one price) and charter flights to the Spanish coast (the Costa Brava and Costa del Sol), the Balearic islands, Italy and Greece boomed from the 1960s and brought the Mediterranean within reach of workers from northern Europe.
Club Méditerranée (Club Med), founded in 1950, offered all-inclusive holidays.
Car ownership made domestic holidays and weekend trips possible, and camping and caravanning became popular in Britain and Scandinavia.
Leisure at home and nearby included spectator sport, cinema, television, record-buying and home improvement, which show the rise of mass leisure industries.
notes.tip: For the consumer society, add holidays to goods and cars. Use the French holiday dates as your precise example and avoid claiming the same dates for all of Western Europe.

notes.b: In the communist states of Eastern Europe, women's employment and legal equality were promoted by the state, but there was little consumer choice and no free feminist movement. Comparing East and West is a good way to show what these changes meant.
points: In the East many more women went out to work, backed by state childcare and the expectation that they would work. Communist states promoted equal rights in law.
Domestic responsibilities for housework and childcare remained largely with women, who therefore carried a double burden of paid work and housework.
East Germany offered state nurseries, paid maternity leave and a 'baby year' from 1976. Abortion was legalised there in 1972, and the divorce rate was high.

In the Soviet Union abortion was legalised again in 1955, and women formed a large part of the workforce, including doctors and engineers. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963, an achievement, but women still did most of the housework.
There was no independent feminist movement in the East, so the Western movement of the 1960s and 1970s had no equivalent there.

Consumer goods in the East were scarcer and of lower quality, so the consumer society was far less developed than in the West. East German cars such as the Trabant and Wartburg had waiting lists of many years.
East German holidays were organised by the trade union federation in union holiday homes and Baltic resorts, and Black Sea resorts served the Soviet bloc, while travel to the West was restricted.
East Germans could watch West German television, so they were conscious of the gap in goods.
notes.tip: Comparing East and West is rewarded. Make the point that legal equality and female employment were similar, but consumer goods differed and there was no free feminist movement in the East. 'Double burden' is the key concept. Do not use Tereshkova as proof of equality; she is an achievement set against the double burden.

notes.b: Historians debate whether the changes of the period liberated women and families or extended consumer pressures into private life. Good answers set achievements against limits and give a judgement.
points: Achievements: legal and employment equality, access to contraception and abortion in many states, easier divorce and more choice in marriage.

Limits: women still bore most domestic work, a pay gap persisted, many women worked in low-paid jobs, and gains were uneven across countries and social classes. In the East there was equality in law but not at home.
Consumerism brought higher living standards and more leisure, but critics argued that it encouraged conformity, debt through credit and pressure to buy, and that it tied family life to paid work.
Contemporaries disagreed: churches and conservatives defended the traditional family, while feminists demanded new rights.
Later historians see the 1960s and 1970s as a turning point, but they stress that the gains were uneven.
notes.tip: Give a stated judgement organised by theme (work, law, reproduction, family), with dated laws and named people. Explanations of why change came score more than lists of laws.

keyTerms.definition: A movement and set of ideas that argue for equal rights and opportunities for women, and that challenge the social roles assigned to them.
A society in which the purchase of goods and services plays a central role in economic life and in people's identities.
A condition of widespread rising incomes that allowed many households to buy consumer goods and enjoy leisure time.
The sharp rise in birth rates in Western countries from about 1946 to the mid-1960s.
The principle that men and women should receive the same pay for work of equal value, enshrined in Article 119 of the Treaty of Rome.
Loans and hire purchase arrangements that allowed households to buy goods before paying for them in full.
The women's movement of the 1960s and 1970s that campaigned for equal pay, reproductive rights and an end to the social roles that confined women to the home.
A holiday sold as a single price covering travel, accommodation and sometimes meals, which brought foreign travel within reach of workers from the 1960s.
Simone de Beauvoir's 1949 book arguing that women were defined as the Other by a male-centred society.
